target.title: RFC: Readiness Conditions and Providers
target.body:
## Decision requested

Should OpenClaw modernize its existing fixed Gateway readiness evaluator into one structured, extensible condition contract?

This RFC covers **readiness conditions and providers only**. Standard Hosting Profiles have moved to a separate RFC so the readiness facility can be accepted and used independently.

## Implementer specification

The normative V1 contract is the [Readiness v1 specification](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/rfcs/blob/user/giodl/standard-hosting-profiles-ready-check/rfcs/0018/readiness-v1-spec.md). The RFC carries the design rationale and rollout plan; the sidecar is the schema, provider lifecycle, bounded evaluation, projection, and conformance reference.

## Problem

OpenClaw already exposes `/ready` and `/readyz`, but the evaluator is purpose-built around a fixed set of Gateway observations. Today:

- startup, drain, channel, and event-loop observations do not share one iterable condition shape;
- plugins cannot contribute bounded readiness observations;
- operators cannot explicitly require a known plugin-owned dependency;
- health and status may omit or represent readiness facts differently; and
- hosts add private scripts for missing facts such as workspace writability.

The result is ambiguity between "the process responds" and "this runtime can accept work."

## Proposed v1

Every observation uses one stable shape:

```text
type + status + requirement + reason + message
```

- Required `False` or `Unknown` conditions fail readiness.
- Advisory conditions remain visible without causing an outage.
- Existing Gateway startup, drain, channel, and event-loop observations become canonical core conditions.
- Existing `failing`, `suppressed`, and `eventLoop` fields remain compatibility projections.
- `/ready`, `/readyz`, health, status, and an optional CLI project the same result.
- `/healthz` remains shallow liveness.

## Direct use without profiles

The RFC is directly useful on its own. Universal Gateway lifecycle conditions always apply; an operator may explicitly add registered core or plugin criteria as required or advisory:

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    readiness: {
      requiredCriteria: [
        "openclaw.workspace-writable",
        "plugin.storage.backend",
      ],
      advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
    },
  },
}
```

Registering a criterion does not make it a blocker. Existing installations do not acquire new required workspace or plugin dependencies. Only explicit operator configuration, or a separately selected hosting profile, adds requirements beyond the universal baseline.

## Plugin providers

Only activated plugins may register executable providers through `OpenClawPluginApi`. Operators reference IDs; they cannot inject callbacks through config.

Providers are:

- activation-scoped and atomically replaced on reload;
- namespaced and enumerable without exposing callbacks;
- observational, read-only, and idempotent;
- advisory by default;
- bounded by per-provider deadlines and an outer watchdog; and
- converted to stable `Unknown` results on timeout or error.

Core retains ownership of invocation, cancellation, coalescing, caching, validation, redaction, and result ordering. If a callback ignores cancellation after its deadline, later polls reuse the stable timeout result and do not start duplicate work. If the canonical evaluator itself times out or fails, every projection receives a redacted required `ReadinessEvaluationComplete=Unknown` condition rather than a rejected health/status request.

## Compatibility and boundaries

This proposal extends existing Gateway readiness. It does not add a second health service, policy engine, OCC dependency, hosting abstraction, or config system.

It does not define profile names, profile selection, activation identity, or release profile conformance. Those product/support decisions are isolated in the Standard Hosting Profiles RFC.

Readiness also remains distinct from state continuity: `/ready` says whether this runtime can serve work now; it does not prove checkpoint durability or safe destruction.

## Primary implementation

The primary implementation to review is [openclaw/openclaw#104018](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018). It is the proposed upstream landing shape: one draft PR with four ordered commits at exact head `17b34f792d8`, rebased onto OpenClaw `main` at `4e78d91c0f9`, with exact-head tests, published-upgrade evidence, and package-installed Docker proof.

The fork PRs below expose those same commits as optional smaller review slices. They are supporting review aids, not alternative landing PRs:

| Slice | Draft PR | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Canonical core conditions | [PR 17](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17) | Normalize existing Gateway observations and compatibility projections. |
| Workspace readiness | [PR 22](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22) | Add one bounded core criterion without profile behavior. |
| Readiness providers and explicit requirements | [PR 23](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23) | Add plugin registration and direct `gateway.readiness` selection. |
| Canonical readiness CLI | [PR 27](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27) | Add `openclaw ready` as a thin projection of the live result. |

The [consolidated draft implementation](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018) contains the same four review slices. Its exact package proves `/ready` and `/readyz` transition `200 -> 503 -> 200`, `/healthz` remains live, and `openclaw ready --json` exits `0 -> 1 -> 0` with the same canonical condition. A published `2026.7.1 -> 2026.7.2` upgrade lane also proves existing installations retain their readiness baseline instead of silently acquiring opt-in criteria.

## Maintainer questions

1. Is the required/advisory condition model the right modernization of the existing evaluator?
2. Is activation-scoped plugin registration the right extension boundary?
3. Is explicit `gateway.readiness` selection sufficient for v1 without profiles?

Profile naming, profile support ownership, runtime activation identity, and release conformance can now be reviewed independently.

target.title: RFC 0023: Standard Hosting Profiles
target.body:
## Review purpose

This is the separate product/support follow-up to [RFC 0018: Readiness Conditions and Providers](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/33). RFC 0018 is directly useful without profiles: operators can select required or advisory readiness criteria themselves. This RFC asks whether OpenClaw should also ship a small catalog of named, release-tested runtime postures over that same facility.

## Implementer specification

The normative V1 contract is the [Standard Hosting Profile v1 specification](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/rfcs/blob/user/giodl/rfc-0023-standard-hosting-profiles/rfcs/0023/hosting-profile-v1-spec.md). The RFC carries the product and support rationale; the sidecar is the exact profile catalog, selection, activation, extension, projection, and packaged-conformance reference.

## Problem

OpenClaw runs locally, in containers, behind identity proxies, and as a controller for paired execution targets, but those broad deployment labels are not reproducible support contracts. Today the intended posture is spread across startup flags, environment, config, container probes, adapter code, and private checklists. A running Gateway cannot name the posture it is expected to satisfy, and a packaged release cannot prove that posture as a coherent scenario.

## Proposal

Ship four standard profiles:

| Profile | Supported posture | Additional required evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | Explicit foreground or local Gateway posture | Universal Gateway readiness plus writable workspace |
| `container` | Directly reachable container listener | Non-loopback effective listener |
| `reverse-proxy` | Gateway behind a trusted identity proxy | Trusted-proxy auth, user header, and trusted source |
| `node-mode` | Gateway controlling one or more execution targets | Approved pairing, connected target, command grant, and control channel |

A profile is declarative data that composes RFC 0018 conditions. It does not create another evaluator, generate config, encode scheduler policy, or make a host/control plane part of OpenClaw core. Selection is optional and opt-in, so an upgrade preserves the existing unprofiled readiness baseline:

```text
gateway startup argument > environment > openclaw.json
```

Without a selection, OpenClaw adds neither `ProfileSelected` nor profile-only requirements. Operators opt into a standard support posture through config, environment, or the Gateway startup argument.

## Why this is a support contract

The standard catalog gives maintainers and operators one reproducible claim:

```text
OpenClaw names the supported runtime posture.
The runtime reports the exact conditions and activation being evaluated.
The release process executes that posture against the packaged artifact.
Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and downstream hosts consume ordinary readiness.
```

The proposal also defines logical runtime and unique incarnation identity so readiness evidence can be attributed to one activation. Operator profiles may extend, but cannot weaken, a standard baseline; OpenClaw owns only the conformance promise for its standard catalog.

## Implementation evidence

- Readiness dependency: [openclaw/openclaw#104018](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018)
- Upstream profile implementation: [openclaw/openclaw#107765](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107765), exact head `f54affa3983`, stacked on readiness head `17b34f792d8` from PR 104018
- Profile-only comparison view: [giodl73-repo/openclaw#94](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/94)
- Profile-only implementation size: 32 files, 1,343 insertions, 5 deletions, including docs and tests
- Validation: 273 focused assertions plus formatting, type-aware lint, diff, package, and exact-head Docker matrix checks pass; the unrelated `sessions.abort` timeout reproduces on the exact readiness base

PR 107765 contains the exact readiness head followed by eight ordered profile commits covering the standard catalog, node-mode, runtime activation identity, packaged conformance, startup lifecycle safety, host-provisioned workspace proof, real node approval proof, and explicit opt-in compatibility. Until PR 104018 lands, GitHub shows both layers in its aggregate diff; afterward the PR naturally reduces to the profile-only change. Fork PR 94 provides that clean profile-only comparison now. Fork PRs [#18](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18), [#19](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19), [#42](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/42), and [#21](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/21) expose the major design slices as optional review aids.

The exact package-installed matrix first proves that an unprofiled package remains `200` without profile-only conditions, then passes explicit `local`, `container`, `reverse-proxy`, and `node-mode`, including listener/auth failures, workspace full/recovery, and the existing node approval flow. Proof image: `sha256:20d507b613b346e1165add88234eb00390ea6d1b086970dd3589dd3f41654175`.

## Promotion order

1. Accept and land RFC 0018/readiness first.
2. Decide RFC 0023 independently as the standard profile and support-matrix contract.
3. Let PR 107765 reduce to its eight profile-only commits, refresh proof against the landed readiness contract, and review it for landing.

## Review questions

1. Are these four postures the right initial standard catalog?
2. Should runtime activation identity remain in the initial profile contract?
3. Should packaged profile conformance become release-blocking when the contract is accepted?
